issues.issue: The lessor is recited as "a married man and acting in his sole and separate interest," without his spouse joining, leaving open whether any marital or entireties interest is bound. The phrase does not identify what interest is being leased.

The grant of the right to "transport by pipelines or otherwise across and through said lands oil, gas and their constituents from the subject and other lands," surviving the lease term, cannot be squared with Paragraph 25 and Addendum ¶20, which deny Lessee the right to move foreign gas across the premises. The Addendum priority clause sharpens which controls.

The premises are described both by enumerated tax parcels with stated acreages and by a catch-all covering "all the property owned by Lessor or to which the Lessor may have any rights" in the section and adjoining sections. Whether the specific parcels or the general words bound the leasehold is a general-versus-specific question.

The habendum extends the term so long as gas is "produced or are capable of being produced on the premises in paying quantities, in the judgment of the Lessee"; "capable of being produced" and "paying quantities" are undefined and left to Lessee's judgment. Whether the lease survives without marketed production turns on that phrase.

The term is continued "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," but Paragraph 7 speaks only to the adequacy of consideration and Lessee's right to drill or not drill; the shut-in mechanism is Paragraph 6. The cross-reference cannot be given effect as written.

A well is deemed "commenced when preparations for drilling have been commenced," while Addendum ¶16 defines commencement of operations as entry with road-building equipment followed by a drilling rig for spudding. The two definitions cannot both govern.

Lessee may elect to pay "the market price for such one-eighth royalty oil at the published rate for oil of like grade and gravity," without identifying the publication, market or valuation point. "Market price" and "published rate" have no benchmark in the instrument.

Gas royalty is one-eighth of "the price paid to Lessee," and the following post-production-cost deduction language is struck through, so whether royalty is net or gross of gathering, transportation, dehydration and compression is unresolved. "The price paid to Lessee" is itself undefined for affiliate sales.

This subparagraph lets Lessee deduct "Lessor's share of any severance or other tax imposed by any government body" from royalty, which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶14 making Lessee responsible for increases in property taxes levied on Lessor because of its operations. The Addendum priority clause puts the two against each other.

The payee line is not completed — payment is to be made "to the order of and mailed to: LESSOR at ABOVE ADDRESS" — so "the said named person" who is to continue as Lessor's agent is never named. Who holds the agency to receive payments after a change of ownership is left blank.

Paragraph 6 provides a shut-in royalty but never says that paying it keeps the lease in force, which must be read against Paragraph 2's habendum extending the term while gas is "capable of being produced." Whether shut-in payments hold the lease past the primary term is unresolved between the two.

Paragraph 2 continues the term "as provided in Paragraph 7 following," yet this paragraph supplies only an acknowledgment of consideration and a right to drill or not drill. Paragraph 7 cannot perform the function Paragraph 2 assigns it.

Pooling is capped at 640 acres "or such larger unit as may be required by state law or regulation," a trigger with no applicable boundary in Pennsylvania, and Lessee must "maintain a well density of at least 1 well per 160 acres contained in such unit." Both the size limit and the density duty are indeterminate as written.

Paragraph 9 divides royalties among several owners in proportion to acreage owned of the entire leased acreage, while Paragraph 8 allocates royalty on the acreage consolidated into a development unit. Which allocation governs a pooled tract with multiple owners is left to be reconciled.

No change in Lessor's ownership binds Lessee until it receives "certified copies of all recorded instruments or documents and other information necessary to establish a complete chain of record title," leaving Lessee to judge what is necessary and complete. The standard for effective notice is undefined.

"Lessor agrees that when and if the within lease is assigned, the Lessee herein shall have no further obligations hereunder" does not say whether accrued liabilities and continuing covenants are released along with future ones. The scope of the release on assignment is the defect.

The paragraph has Lessor waive "notice of any assignment or transfer of the within lease," which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶17 requiring Lessee to give written notice of any assignment of 51% or more within fourteen days. The Addendum priority clause makes the conflict live.

The paragraph sends "any damages if not mutually agreed upon" to three disinterested appraisers and then states "Arbitration shall be mandatory," without saying whether that covers only damage valuation or every dispute under the lease. Whether this is an appraisal clause or an arbitration agreement is the ambiguity.

Lessor must "abide by all reasonable safety policies of Lessee," policies made unilaterally by Lessee and nowhere identified, with "reasonable" left unmeasured. The setbacks are given as "including but not limited to," so the obligation has no stated outer limit.

Surrender is declared "a cancellation of all liabilities under the same of each and all parties hereto," which cannot be squared with Addendum ¶¶1–2 imposing repair and restoration duties that by their terms follow the cessation of operations. Whether surrender wipes out accrued restoration obligations is the conflict.

The clause reduces "the land rental hereinbefore set forth" in proportion to acreage surrendered, but Paragraph 3 makes this a paid-up lease and no land rental is set forth anywhere. The reduction mechanism has no antecedent.

The clause provides that "in no event shall the within lease expire for a period of ninety (90) days after the termination of any force majeure," wording that postpones expiration rather than extending the term, and the triggering events are an open-ended "including but not limited to" list. What counts as force majeure and how long it tolls the term are both uncertain.

Notice is made "precedent to the bringing of any action by Lessor on said lease for any cause," and Lessee need only "meet or commence to meet all or any part of the breaches" within thirty days. Whether the requirement bars all claims and what suffices to commence to meet a breach are undefined.

Lessor promises to grant "no other lease for the minerals covered by this lease," which sits against Addendum ¶21 stating that Lessee has not acquired coalbed methane rights without Lessor's prior written consent. Whether Lessor may lease coalbed methane elsewhere turns on reading the two together.

The warranty that there are no "commercially producing wells currently existing" leaves "commercially producing" undefined. What output or profitability makes a well commercially producing is fixed nowhere in the lease.

The option sets no deadline by which Lessee must exercise it, saying only that the additional five-year term commences "on the date that the lease would have expired but for the extension." It also cross-refers to "Paragraph numbered 6" for the method of payment, although Paragraph 6 states a shut-in royalty and Paragraph 5 supplies the payment method.

The provision declares that "no implied covenant, agreement or obligation shall be read into this agreement," which must be reconciled with Paragraph 4(B)'s royalty measured on "the price paid to Lessee," a measure presupposing a duty to market. Whether the disclaimer defeats implied marketing and development covenants is the question.

Paragraph 21 covers Clean and Green assessments caused by Lessee's operations, while Addendum ¶13 covers the same ground and adds the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program. The two overlapping promises differ in scope, and the Addendum priority clause requires a choice between them.

Lessee indemnifies Lessor for all claims arising from its operations "unless such damage or injury is caused solely by Lessor's acts, omissions, or negligence," which by negative implication reaches losses to which Lessor's negligence contributed. Whether the clause indemnifies Lessor against his own negligence is not expressed.

Paragraph 23 requires locations to be fixed "by mutual consent between Lessor and Lessee," while Addendum ¶3 substitutes a written approval form with deemed approval if Lessor is silent for thirty days. Mutual consent and deemed consent cannot both control the same decision.

Thirty days' notice is given "to allow the Lessor to harvest any marketable timber, or domesticated crops," without defining "marketable" or saying what follows if thirty days does not suffice. The extent of Lessor's harvesting right is vague.

This paragraph bars Lessee from asserting the right to transport gas from other lands across the premises, which cannot be squared with the Paragraph 1 grant of exactly that right, expressly surviving the lease term. One of the two must yield.

The restriction is phrased as an agreement "not to assert the right" rather than a denial of the right, and it lapses "unless the lands covered by this lease are pooled, communitized, or included in a production unit." Whether pooling any part of the tract lifts the restriction entirely is unstated.

This paragraph makes the Addendum part of the lease, while Paragraph 20 declares the instrument contains all the agreements of the parties. Read with the Addendum's own priority clause, the relationship between the two documents must be worked out.

The priority clause makes the Addendum prevail over "the inconsistent provisions of the main body" without identifying which provisions are inconsistent, and it operates against Paragraph 20's integration clause. Whether Paragraph 1's transport and storage grants are "inconsistent" with Addendum ¶¶8, 20 and 21 is exactly what it leaves open.

Addendum ¶1 requires restoration "as nearly as possible" to the condition at commencement of drilling within 90 days "weather permitting," while Addendum ¶2 requires restoration "to as near its original condition as is reasonably possible" with no deadline. Two different standards and baselines govern the same obligation.

Addendum ¶2 measures restoration against the land's "original condition" and sets no time limit, while Addendum ¶1 measures it against the condition at commencement of drilling and requires completion within 90 days. The two cannot both be the operative standard.

Addendum ¶3's approval-form procedure, under which Lessor's silence for thirty days "shall constitute Lessor's approval," cannot be squared with Paragraph 23's requirement of mutual consent to locations. It also obliges Lessor to propose an alternate location that Lessee "deems to be economically feasible."

Addendum ¶4 forbids Lessee to take water from Lessor's ponds, springs or creeks without written consent, while Paragraph 14 gives Lessee the privilege of using sufficient water for operating on the premises. The two cannot both be given full effect.

Addendum ¶5 requires all pipeline laid by Lessee to be buried at least 32 inches, while Paragraph 12 requires burial only "when so requested by the Lessor." Whether burial is automatic or on request is left to be reconciled.

The paragraph caps access roads at 40 feet "during actual drilling operation" and 16 feet for a producing well, without saying which limit applies between drilling and production. Restoration is owed only "as close as is practicable," an unmeasured standard.

Addendum ¶7 imposes a second, differently worded indemnity covering "any penalty or damage or charges imposed for any violation of any laws or ordinances" and all claims and liens arising from acts or omissions of Lessee or those holding under it, overlapping Paragraph 22's indemnity. Paragraph 22 excepts damage caused solely by Lessor's negligence and this one does not, so which governs a claim within both is unresolved.

Addendum ¶8 states Lessee has not acquired rights to drill an underground gas or oil storage well, while Paragraph 1 grants the right of "injecting and storing, air, gas, brine and other substances from any source and into any subsurface strata." The storage grant and the storage denial are in direct conflict.

Addendum ¶9 fixes crop damages at "the current value in the area" of the crop cultivated, while Paragraph 12 sends damages to growing crops to a three-appraiser determination. Which mechanism values crop damage is unresolved.

Addendum ¶10 keeps mechanics' liens off the landowners' royalty interest, while Paragraph 11 lets Lessee pay any lien against Lessor's interest, become subrogated, and direct royalties to satisfying existing liens. The protection and the royalty-diversion right pull against each other.

The water-replacement duty turns on a "material adverse change in the quality of Lessor's water supply," undefined, and only if it occurs "during or immediately after the completion of Lessee's drilling operations." Both the threshold and the window are indeterminate.

Addendum ¶12 repeats the three-appraiser damages procedure of Paragraph 12 but omits the sentence "Arbitration shall be mandatory." Whether the Addendum displaces mandatory arbitration for timber and improvement damages is left open by the priority clause.

Addendum ¶13 duplicates Paragraph 21's Clean and Green indemnity while adding CREP and confining the trigger to operations "on Lessor's lands." Which of the two overlapping promises governs an assessment, and whether the narrower words limit Paragraph 21, must be worked out.

Addendum ¶14 makes Lessee responsible for "any increase in property taxes, if any, levied upon Lessor as a result of Lessee's Oil and Gas operations," which cannot be squared with Paragraph 4(C) authorizing Lessee to deduct from royalty Lessor's share of "any severance or other tax imposed by any government body." The overlap between the two tax provisions is unresolved.

The cash-equivalency formula is incomplete as written — an election to receive "in lieu of payment for an allotment of three hundred thousand cubic feet of gas, a 'cash equivalency' payment times the annualized wellhead price" states no multiplicand or rate. The lease also grants no free-gas allotment for the payment to be in lieu of, Paragraph 8 allowing gas only to the owner of the tract on which the well sits.

Addendum ¶16 defines commencement of operations as entry with equipment to build access roads followed by a drilling rig for spudding, while Paragraph 3 deems a well commenced "when preparations for drilling have been commenced." The two definitions cannot both govern when operations begin.

Addendum ¶17 requires Lessee to give written notice of any assignment resulting in a 51% or greater interest within fourteen days, while Paragraph 11 has Lessor waive notice of any assignment. The waiver and the notice duty are in direct conflict.

The location fee of $2,500.00 is payable "upon commencement of drilling operations on the leased premises" without saying whether it is owed once or for each well drilled. Whether commencement here means what Addendum ¶16 defines or what Paragraph 3 deems is also unstated.

The audit right runs only to "determining the quantity of said gas and/or oil produced, metered and sold from the premises," so it does not on its face reach price or the deductions that fix royalty under Paragraph 4(B). The scope of the audit right is the defect.

Addendum ¶20 denies Lessee the right "to transport foreign gas across the premises described in this lease," which cannot be squared with Paragraph 1's express grant of the right to transport oil and gas from other lands across the leasehold, surviving the term. This is the sharpest conflict in the instrument.

"Foreign gas" is undefined, and the permitted transport reaches gas "produced from the premises described" and from "the premises unitized herewith," leaving unclear how gas from a pooled unit is characterized. What is foreign and what is unitized is the ambiguity.

Addendum ¶21 states that Lessee has not acquired the right to develop or produce coalbed methane gas without Lessor's prior written consent, while Paragraphs 1, 2, 4 and 8 lease coalbed methane gas, measure royalty on it and hold the lease by its production. The grant and the reservation cannot both be given effect.
